foundations.title: What is AI, ML, DL, CNN, and RNN?
foundations.shortDesc: Understand the hierarchy of artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and classic architectures.
foundations.hierarchyTitle: The Hierarchy: AI → Machine Learning → Deep Learning → LLM
foundations.aiDef: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the broad umbrella concept of machines performing tasks that typically require human cognition (reasoning, perception, language, planning).
foundations.mlDef: Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI where systems learn patterns from empirical data rather than relying on explicit hand-crafted rules.
foundations.dlDef: Deep Learning (DL) is a subset of ML utilizing artificial neural networks with multiple stacked layers (deep representations) to extract hierarchical features.
foundations.nnDef: A Neural Network is composed of interconnected nodes (neurons) organized into layers. Each connection has an adjustable numerical weight.
foundations.rnnDef: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) process sequential data (audio, time-series, text) with an internal hidden loop that passes memory from step to step, but suffers from vanishing gradients on long contexts.
foundations.cnnDef: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) apply sliding filter kernels across grid inputs (like images) to detect spatial features (edges, textures, shapes), invariant to position.

training.title: How Training & Inference Work
training.shortDesc: Discover how neural networks learn via the forward pass, loss computation, backpropagation, and how inference generates answers.
training.forwardPass: Forward Pass: Inputs flow layer-by-layer through weighted sums and non-linear activation functions (ReLU, GELU, Sigmoid) to produce an output prediction.
training.lossFunction: Loss Function: Quantifies how wrong the prediction is compared to ground truth (e.g., Mean Squared Error for regression, Cross-Entropy for classification).
training.backpropagation: Backpropagation: Calculates the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight using Calculus (the Chain Rule), flowing backwards from output to input.
training.optimization: Optimization (Gradient Descent & AdamW): Updates weights in the opposite direction of the gradient to minimize the loss over epochs.
training.inference: Inference: The weights are frozen. New unseen inputs are evaluated in a single forward pass. In LLMs, temperature and top-p sampling control the randomness of next-token generation.

transformer.title: What Makes the Transformer Special?
transformer.shortDesc: Why the 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' architecture revolutionized AI and replaced RNNs completely.
transformer.parallelization: Massive Parallelism: Unlike RNNs that must process token-by-token sequentially, Transformers process entire sequences simultaneously during training, unlocking massive GPU scaling.
transformer.legacyRnnDesc: Sequential bottleneck: Token t+1 depends on state from token t. Impossible to parallelize on GPUs.
transformer.transformerParallelDesc: All tokens ingested at once. Computation is framed as large matrix GEMMs running simultaneously across GPU cores.
transformer.selfAttention: Self-Attention Mechanism: Allows every token in a sentence to attend to every other token, calculating contextual relevance dynamically.
transformer.qkv: Query, Key, and Value: Inspired by information retrieval. A token's Query (what it looks for) is compared via dot-product with every other token's Key (what it contains), scaled by sqrt(d_k), passed through Softmax to produce weights, and multiplied by the Values.
transformer.positionalEncoding: Positional Encoding: Since attention is permutation-invariant, positional encodings (sinusoids or modern Rotary Position Embeddings / RoPE) inject sequence order into the vectors.

frontier.title: MoE, FlashAttention, Tokens & Emergent Abilities
frontier.shortDesc: Explore cutting-edge frontier LLM concepts, tokens, tensors, sparse routing, and memory optimization.
frontier.tokens: Tokens: LLMs do not read letters or whole words. They split text into subword chunks called tokens (e.g., Byte-Pair Encoding). 1,000 English words typically equate to ~1,300 tokens.
frontier.tensors: Vectors, Matrices & Tensors: A scalar is 0D, a vector is 1D (token embedding), a matrix is 2D (layer weights), and a tensor is an N-dimensional array holding batches of sequences.
frontier.moe: Mixture of Experts (MoE): Instead of activating all parameters for every token, a gating network selectively routes each token to top-K expert networks (e.g., activating only 2 out of 8 experts), slashing compute costs while preserving capacity.
frontier.flashAttention: FlashAttention: An exact, hardware-aware attention algorithm that tiles computation across fast on-chip GPU SRAM, avoiding slow High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) read/writes.
frontier.emergentAbilities: Emergent Abilities: Qualitative jumps in capability (multi-step reasoning, coding, theory of mind) that appear as models scale across compute, parameters, and dataset tokens.

timeline.alexnet: Dawn of the modern Deep Learning revolution accelerated by GPUs.
timeline.transformer: Google Brain publishes the foundational architecture underpinning all modern LLMs.
timeline.gpt3: Demonstrates Scaling Laws and emergent In-Context Learning capabilities without fine-tuning.
timeline.chatgpt: The generative AI inflection point bringing LLMs to the mainstream alongside foundational open-weights models.
timeline.moeReasoning: Sparse Mixture of Experts architectures, hardware-aware FlashAttention-3, and test-time chain-of-thought reasoning (o1, DeepSeek, Gemini).

hardware.title: Hardware Bottlenecks, Edge AI & Quantization
hardware.shortDesc: Can your phone or PC run AI? The critical distinction between compute (FLOPs) and memory bandwidth (GB/s).
hardware.canWeRun: Can we run AI locally? Yes! Small efficient LLMs (1B to 8B parameters) run today on modern laptops and smartphones via local inference engines (Ollama, llama.cpp, WebLLM, ONNX Runtime).
hardware.twinBottlenecks: Prefill vs. Generation Bottleneck: Processing your prompt (prefill) is compute-bound (TFLOPs), fully utilizing matrix cores. But outputting text token-by-token is memory-bandwidth bound (GB/s) — the system must read gigabytes of model weights from memory for every single token!
hardware.bandwidthFormula: Generation Speed Formula: Max Tokens/sec = Memory Bandwidth (GB/s) ÷ Model Memory Size (GB). If an 8B model takes 4.5 GB and your laptop has 90 GB/s bandwidth, max speed is ~20 tokens/sec.
hardware.quantizationIntro: Quantization compresses high-precision floating point numbers into fewer bits, slashing memory footprint and bandwidth requirements with minimal loss in reasoning quality.

formats.fp32: FP32 (32-bit): 4 bytes/param. Full single precision, primarily used in research and master training weights.
formats.fp16: FP16 / BF16 (16-bit): 2 bytes/param. Standard format for modern deep learning training and baseline weights.
formats.fp8: FP8 (8-bit): 1 byte/param. Native to Nvidia Hopper H100 and Blackwell GPUs, halving memory bandwidth demands.
formats.int8: INT8 (8-bit integer): 1 byte/param. Popular quantization standard for high accuracy with 50% memory savings.
formats.int4: INT4 (4-bit integer, GGUF/AWQ): 0.5 bytes/param. Enables 7B models to fit in under 4 GB VRAM for laptops and phones.
formats.nvfp4: NVFP4 (4-bit microscopic float): Nvidia Blackwell architecture format offering extreme speedup with 2x throughput over FP8.
